text: Platform Fundamentals already introduced the basic pattern: Development, Test/QA, and Production, with changes promoted between them deliberately, never copied silently. That's the right starting mental model, but real organizations running real applications at scale typically build more structure around it than just three boxes.

A common refinement is a dedicated Build instance, sometimes called an integration or construction instance, sitting between Dev and Test. Developers do their day-to-day work in Dev, where half-finished changes and experiments are normal and expected. Before anything is considered ready for formal Test/QA validation, it's first promoted to Build.

Build is where multiple developers' changes are merged and run together, catching integration problems — two developers touching the same table in conflicting ways, for example — in an environment dedicated to exactly that question, before Test/QA testers ever see it. Dev answers whether your own change works in isolation. Build answers whether everyone's merged changes still work together. Test/QA answers whether it works correctly for a real business tester.

Sub-production instances don't stay static. Over time, a Dev or Test instance's data and configuration drift away from what Production actually looks like — new fields, new records, new real-world edge cases pile up in Production that Dev was never updated to reflect. The standard fix is a periodic clone refresh, quarterly is common, where the organization clones Production's current data into its sub-production instances.

A clone refresh copies everything from Production, including every real customer's real name, email address, and other personal data. That's exactly the scenario data anonymization was built for: a dev or test instance has no legitimate business need to hold real customer PII, and cloning it there anyway multiplies the number of people and systems with access to it, with no real benefit.

A disciplined refresh process applies anonymization immediately after the clone lands, before any developer or tester ever opens the instance — turning "we happened to copy real PII into Dev" into "Dev never actually held real PII at all, by design."
